description: Free full-length narrative plus 1-page NCMHCE answer strategy cheat sheet for lead capture and product preview.

freeNarrative.title: Free Diagnostic Case — Tessa (Generalized Anxiety Disorder)
freeNarrative.presentingProblem:
You are a licensed mental health counselor in outpatient private practice. Your client self-referred after searching online for therapy late one night. She stated, "I’m not in crisis exactly. I’m just exhausted from being myself."

The client is a 29-year-old marketing project manager who reported chronic, difficult-to-control worry across multiple areas of her life, including work performance, her upcoming wedding, her father’s health, finances, and whether people are disappointed in her. She stated, "My brain acts like every problem is urgent and every mistake is permanent." She reported that this pattern has been present since adolescence but has worsened over the past eight months after being promoted into a role that involves supervising others.

She now checks emails repeatedly before sending them, rereads Slack messages to see whether she sounded rude, and mentally replays meetings at night. She stated, "If my boss says, 'Can we talk tomorrow,' I assume I’m getting fired. Then I spend twelve hours preparing for every possible disaster." She reported fatigue, irritability, muscle tension in her shoulders and jaw, difficulty concentrating, restlessness, and sleep disturbance. She stated that she can fall asleep but wakes around 3:00 a.m. thinking about unfinished tasks or possible future problems.

She reported feeling embarrassed that she appears competent externally while feeling "like a fraud with a nervous system problem" internally. Her fiancé has encouraged therapy because she becomes tearful, snappy, and withdrawn during periods of high stress. She denied panic attacks, though she described several moments of feeling "right on the edge of losing it" during which her chest feels tight and she fears she may cry at work. When asked what she means by "losing it," she stated, "Not like I’m going to hurt myself or someone else. More like I’m going to stop being able to keep all the plates spinning and everyone will see I’m not okay."

She denied any history of self-harm, suicide attempts, mania, psychosis, or substance misuse. She drinks one to two glasses of wine on weekends and denied other substances. She denied trauma history beyond what she described as growing up with a father who was loving but unpredictable because of untreated diabetes and periodic hospitalizations. She stated, "I learned early that if I stayed prepared, things felt less scary."

She reported that her mother was "a worrier too" and often asked her as a child whether doors were locked, assignments were done, or if something bad might happen to her father. The client stated that friends describe her as dependable, organized, and driven, but she experiences those same qualities as "fear dressed up as competence." She came to treatment now because she is tired of feeling physically tense all the time and because she worries that marriage, future parenthood, and increasing work responsibility will make her symptoms worse.
freeNarrative.mentalStatusObservation:
Your client presented in neat business attire and appeared her stated age. She was alert and fully oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Grooming and hygiene were good. Eye contact was consistent. Speech was clear, coherent, and mildly fast at times, especially when discussing work stress. Mood was reported as "stressed all the time." Affect was anxious but appropriate and reactive. Psychomotor activity was notable for fidgeting with her ring and periodically rubbing the back of her neck.

Thought processes were linear, logical, and goal-directed, though notably preoccupied with future-oriented worry. Thought content reflected fear of failure, perfectionism, and anticipatory anxiety. There was no evidence of delusions, hallucinations, or formal thought disorder. She denied current suicidal or homicidal ideation. Insight was fair to good; she recognized that her worry is excessive but reported feeling unable to shut it off. Judgment appeared intact. She denied substance misuse. She reported chronic shoulder tension, jaw clenching, headaches, and nonrestorative sleep but no acute medical concerns.
freeNarrative.familyHistory: The client is the older of two daughters. She described her mother as loving, highly responsible, and chronically anxious, though never formally diagnosed. Her father is a retired electrician with longstanding diabetes that was poorly managed during the client’s childhood, resulting in several frightening hospitalizations. She reported that the family often organized itself around preventing crises. She described no family history of bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, or completed suicide. Her younger sister has seen a therapist for panic symptoms in college. The client remains close with both parents and her sister, though she often feels cast in the role of "the capable one."
freeNarrative.workHistory: The client earned a bachelor’s degree in communications and has worked in marketing and project coordination roles for the past seven years. She was promoted eight months ago to project manager at a mid-sized healthcare technology company. She supervises three direct reports and coordinates deadlines across multiple departments. Her performance reviews have been strong, but she reported spending excessive time checking work, preparing for unlikely problems, and trying to anticipate others’ needs. She has not disclosed mental health concerns at work and worries that doing so would make her appear weak or incapable.
freeNarrative.intakeSessionSummary:
You completed a thorough intake and administered the GAD-7, on which the client scored 16, consistent with severe anxiety symptoms. You also administered the PHQ-9, on which she scored 9, reflecting mild depressive symptoms likely secondary to chronic anxiety and poor sleep. You conducted a direct risk assessment in response to her statement about feeling near the edge of "losing it"; she denied suicidal ideation, self-harm urges, homicidal ideation, and history of attempts.

You discussed the diagnosis of Generalized Anxiety Disorder and reviewed evidence-based treatment options, including CBT, worry monitoring, cognitive restructuring, behavioral experiments, and relaxation training. You normalized that high-functioning anxiety can still create meaningful impairment and physical distress. The client expressed relief at feeling understood and stated, "I thought therapy might tell me to just calm down better. This feels more specific than that." You scheduled weekly sessions and provided a worry log for the week.

questions.stem: Tessa has just clarified that 'losing it' does not mean suicidal or homicidal intent — she means losing her capacity to hold everything together. What is the MOST appropriate next step?
options: Reflect the meaning she just offered and ask her to describe what 'losing it' looks like in her body, behavior, and choices when it peaks
Administer the GAD-7 now to anchor a measurable baseline before continuing with the intake narrative
Normalize that high-functioning professionals often describe overload this way and offer brief psychoeducation about the worry cycle
Document her denial of suicidal and homicidal ideation and continue gathering history per the intake template
questions.explanation: Best (A): She has just opened a meaningful self-disclosure. The most therapeutic next move is to deepen her own definition before pivoting to instruments, education, or admin — that becomes the working model you and she share. Second-best (B): A baseline is appropriate this session, but sequencing it ahead of exploration treats her like a data point. (C) Psychoeducation is correct content delivered at the wrong moment — it closes a door she just opened. (D) Documenting and moving on is defensible from a risk standpoint but skips clinical depth. NCMHCE pattern: when a client volunteers meaning, follow the meaning before reaching for a tool.

questions.stem: Tessa says, 'I'm exhausted from being myself.' Which response BEST balances empathy with therapeutic depth?
options: What has it been like carrying this level of tension for so long?
It sounds like the version of you other people see is not the version you actually live with.
Say more about what 'being yourself' is costing you.
I hear how tired you are — that exhaustion makes sense given everything you're holding.
questions.explanation: Best (B): Advanced empathy that names the implicit split between her public self and her internal experience — this is the wound under the sentence. Second-best (A): A warm open invitation, but it puts the burden back on her to find the depth. (C) A useful probe that asks her to explain rather than feel understood. (D) Validation that lands, but does not move the work forward. All four are therapeutic; only one reflects underlying meaning at depth.

questions.stem: Which DSM-5-TR diagnosis BEST fits Tessa's presentation, and what is the strongest reason to favor it over a close competitor?
options: Generalized Anxiety Disorder — excessive, hard-to-control worry across multiple domains, more days than not for years, with required somatic features
Social Anxiety Disorder — much of her worry centers on how she is perceived (replaying conversations, fearing she sounded rude, rereading emails)
Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder — repeated email checking and message rereading function as compulsions tied to intrusive fears
Adjustment Disorder with Anxiety — symptoms escalated after the promotion eight months ago and are stressor-linked
questions.explanation: Best (A): Her worry is uncontrollable, broad (work, fiancé, father, the dog, finances), chronic (years), and accompanied by required GAD somatic features (tension, sleep disturbance, fatigue, restlessness). Second-best (B): Social evaluation is *part* of her picture, but it is not the only or primary axis of her worry. (C) The checking is *worry-driven*, not ego-dystonic intrusions followed by ritualized neutralization — that distinction rules OCD out as primary. (D) The promotion intensified symptoms but did not create them; her pattern predates it by years, which exceeds Adjustment Disorder's 6-month window. NCMHCE pattern: pick the diagnosis that explains the *most* of the picture, not the one that fits one slice.

questions.stem: Which CBT-for-GAD element should be sequenced FIRST in Tessa's treatment plan?
options: Cognitive restructuring of her catastrophic predictions about being fired
Applied relaxation and diaphragmatic breathing to lower her chronic somatic arousal
Psychoeducation about the worry cycle paired with collaborative worry monitoring via a daily log
Graduated behavioral experiments in which she tolerates uncertainty without reassurance-seeking
questions.explanation: Best (C): Every protocolized CBT-for-GAD model opens with a shared conceptualization (psychoeducation) and a baseline (self-monitoring). Without these, the other interventions land in a vacuum and she cannot tell whether they are working. Second-best (B): Relaxation is appropriate early, but it treats the symptom before she understands the cycle that produces it. (A) Cognitive restructuring works once she can catch a worry in real time — which requires the monitoring from (C) first. (D) Experiments are powerful but premature before she has a working model of the mechanism they are testing. All four are real components; sequencing is the test.

questions.stem: Tessa replays conversations at night to check whether she sounded rude. This is BEST conceptualized as:
options: A safety behavior preventing corrective learning about how others actually perceived her
Post-event processing functioning as covert mental checking that maintains the anxiety cycle
A compulsion that warrants exposure and response prevention targeting mental checking
Cognitive rumination consistent with an emerging comorbid depressive process
questions.explanation: Best (B): 'Post-event processing' is the precise transdiagnostic label for repetitive mental review after a social interaction; framing it as *covert checking* names the maintenance mechanism you will target. Second-best (A): True — it is also a safety behavior — but that label is broader and less actionable than naming the specific process. (C) Importing OCD language overpathologizes a worry-driven behavior; her checking is ego-syntonic worry, not intrusion + neutralization. (D) Rumination is depression-coded; nothing in the case supports a depressive comorbidity, so adding it muddies the formulation.

sections.sectionNarrative:
Your client arrived on time and completed the worry log consistently. Her GAD-7 this week is 13, down from 16 at intake. She reported that identifying her worry themes has been helpful but also "humbling" because she had not realized how often she catastrophizes. She stated, "I can turn literally anything into a five-step disaster scenario in under thirty seconds."

She described one recent example: her fiancé did not answer a text for two hours while at work, and she went from mild concern to imagining he had been in a car accident or had changed his mind about their relationship. By the time he called back, she was angry, tearful, and ashamed. She stated, "He was just in a meeting. I acted like I had survived a crisis that never happened."

She also reported increased awareness of how much reassurance she seeks from others, especially her fiancé and her mother. She asks whether they are upset, whether things are okay, and whether she handled situations correctly. She stated, "It helps for ten minutes, then I need it again."

At work, she has begun experimenting with sending emails after one review instead of four and has found that "nothing catastrophic happened," though she still feels highly tense when doing it. She asked you directly, "How do I stop needing certainty all the time? Because I know that’s what I’m really chasing."

questions.stem: Tessa asks how to stop needing certainty all the time. Which intervention BEST targets the underlying mechanism?
options: Schedule a daily 20-minute 'worry time' so worry is contained to a defined window
Use Socratic questioning to examine the evidence behind each catastrophic prediction as it arises
Plan graduated, in-vivo experiments in which she deliberately tolerates uncertainty without seeking reassurance, and tracks what actually happens
Teach mindfulness defusion so she can notice the urge for certainty without automatically acting on it
questions.explanation: Best (C): Intolerance of uncertainty is the engine of GAD. Only experiments where she *deliberately sits with not knowing* directly extinguish the loop she is asking about. Second-best (D): Defusion supports tolerance but does not produce new learning about outcomes the way an experiment does. (B) Socratic work targets the *content* of each worry; she could win every debate and still need certainty. (A) Worry time contains the symptom; it does not address why uncertainty feels intolerable. All four are real interventions; only one targets the mechanism she named.

questions.stem: Reassurance from her fiancé relieves Tessa's anxiety for about ten minutes, then it returns. From a behavioral standpoint, this pattern is BEST described as:
options: Negative reinforcement of reassurance-seeking — the brief relief strengthens the behavior and maintains the anxiety cycle
Intermittent reinforcement that makes the reassurance-seeking especially resistant to extinction
A two-factor process in which short-term relief blocks habituation to the feared outcome
A safety behavior that prevents disconfirmation of her catastrophic prediction
questions.explanation: Best (A): The cleanest behavioral label for the immediate relief-then-repeat loop. Anxiety drops, the drop *reinforces* the seeking, and the behavior strengthens. Second-best (D): Also accurate — reassurance-seeking is a safety behavior — but that frames the *function* rather than the *mechanism* of reinforcement the question asks about. (C) Two-factor theory is more typically applied to phobic avoidance; it overstates what's happening here. (B) Intermittent reinforcement applies if reassurance only *sometimes* helps; the case describes consistent short-term relief, which is straightforward negative reinforcement.

questions.stem: Tessa says, 'I acted like I survived a crisis that never happened.' Which response BEST supports therapeutic depth and the alliance?
options: What was happening inside you in those two hours before he called back?
It sounds like part of you is harsh with the part of you that was scared.
That's the anxiety brain — it treats *possible* like *actual*. Your body was responding to a real threat signal.
Let's map that two-hour spiral on a thought record so we can see the chain from trigger to behavior.
questions.explanation: Best (B): Names the self-criticism inside her sentence — that contempt for the part of her that was frightened is the active wound and the leverage point. Second-best (A): A good exploratory question, but it asks her to *describe* rather than to *feel met*. (C) Psychoeducation that is true and well-timed but moves to teaching before she has been understood. (D) A solid CBT move, but technique offered too soon can feel like the counselor sidestepping the emotional content.

questions.stem: Tessa has begun sending work emails after one review instead of four. From a CBT standpoint, this is MOST accurately described as:
options: Exposure with response prevention targeting a checking behavior
A behavioral experiment that tests her catastrophic prediction by reducing a safety behavior
Successful cognitive restructuring, evidenced by a change in her observable action
Habituation to email-related anxiety through repeated, graduated exposure
questions.explanation: Best (B): In CBT-for-GAD, deliberately reducing a safety behavior to *test a prediction* ('something bad will happen if I don't reread') is called a behavioral experiment. The label captures both the action and its hypothesis-testing function. Second-best (A): ERP language belongs to OCD protocols; using it here implies an intrusion-compulsion frame that does not fit her worry-driven checking. (D) Habituation describes anxiety decreasing through exposure alone; her change is driven by *new learning* about outcomes, not just repetition. (C) Restructuring would have to happen at the cognitive level; the case describes a behavioral change first, which then updates the cognition.

questions.stem: Tessa's fiancé emails you directly to ask how he can best support her between sessions. What is the MOST appropriate response?
options: Do not respond to the email; raise the contact at the next session, let Tessa decide whether and how to involve him, and then act on her direction
Reply that you cannot confirm or discuss her treatment, and invite him to a future joint session contingent on Tessa's written consent
Send a brief, generic reply with publicly available psychoeducation about anxiety so nothing client-specific is disclosed
Forward the email to Tessa so she sees it directly and can decide whether to reply or bring it to session
questions.explanation: Best (A): Preserves confidentiality, protects the therapeutic frame, and centers Tessa's autonomy. The contact becomes clinical material she controls. Second-best (B): Defensible, but *replying at all* — even to decline — confirms a treatment relationship and opens a direct channel with a third party before she has consented. (C) A generic reply feels safe but still creates an outside-of-session channel and subtly aligns you with him. (D) Forwarding hands her the problem without the therapeutic processing she is paying you for. NCMHCE pattern: in third-party-contact items, the answer is almost always *do not act unilaterally; route the decision through the client*.

sections.sectionNarrative:
Your client arrived for her tenth session reporting meaningful improvement. Her GAD-7 score is now 8. She stated, "I still worry, but it doesn’t run the whole day anymore." She has been sleeping better on most nights and reports fewer headaches and less jaw tension.

She described a recent success: her supervisor scheduled a last-minute meeting, and although she noticed the familiar thought that she might be in trouble, she used the cognitive and behavioral strategies you had practiced rather than spiraling into all-night worry. The meeting turned out to be about a new project lead opportunity.

She also reported a more difficult moment from the previous weekend. Her father had a hypoglycemic episode at home and briefly scared the family. The client noticed herself immediately reverting to old roles — taking charge, overfunctioning, and mentally preparing for every possible medical outcome. She stated, "For two days it felt like I was fourteen again and the whole job was to hold everything together."

She was able to notice the pattern, name it, and use paced breathing and scheduled worry time, but she felt discouraged that the old intensity returned so quickly. She asked, "Does this mean I’m back at square one whenever real life happens?"

questions.stem: Tessa asks whether her symptom spike means she is 'back at square one.' Which response is MOST therapeutic?
options: Setbacks are a normal part of recovery and don't erase the work you've done.
Notice that you recognized the pattern, named it, and used your skills — that is very different from where you were at intake.
What would it mean about you if it did mean you were back at square one?
Let's look at the data: your GAD-7 dropped from 16 to 8, which objectively shows progress.
questions.explanation: Best (B): Validates without dismissing *and* points to the specific behavior that proves the mechanism of change is now hers. That consolidates the gain rather than just reassuring her. Second-best (C): A strong schema-level question, but at this moment she needs the spike contextualized before she can do that work. (A) True and warm, but generic — could be said to any client about any setback. (D) Data-based and accurate, yet showing her the chart can feel like a rebuttal of her feeling rather than a response to it.

questions.stem: Tessa's response to her father's hypoglycemic episode is BEST conceptualized as:
options: State-dependent reactivation of an early family role under a salient cue, not a return of the underlying disorder
A core schema around responsibility and overcontrol flaring under stress, indicating schema-focused work should now be added
A trauma response suggesting PTSD criteria should be reassessed given her caregiving history
Anticipatory anxiety indicating that GAD symptoms are returning and the treatment plan should be intensified
questions.explanation: Best (A): The reaction is cue-driven (a real medical event in the parent she has long managed) and time-limited. It reflects an old role lighting up under a matching stimulus — not relapse. Naming it this way preserves treatment gains and gives her a usable frame. Second-best (B): The schema is real and worth noting, but pivoting to schema therapy after one cued episode overcorrects. (D) Reintensifying treatment after a single cue treats a normal reactivation as a recurrence. (C) PTSD requires Criterion A and a symptom cluster the case does not describe; reaching for that label overpathologizes a meaningful but bounded response.

questions.stem: Given a GAD-7 of 8 and consistent skill use, what is the MOST appropriate next phase of treatment?
options: Begin spacing sessions and collaboratively build a written relapse-prevention plan that includes early-warning signs, high-risk situations, skills to deploy, and when to re-engage
Maintain weekly sessions until her GAD-7 is below 5 to ensure full remission before any change in frequency
Add a between-session self-monitoring protocol and reassess in four weeks before changing session frequency
Shift to monthly maintenance sessions focused on consolidation and skill review
questions.explanation: Best (A): Mild-range GAD-7 plus demonstrated skill ownership is exactly the inflection point for tapering paired with a written relapse-prevention plan — the evidence-based standard for ending CBT-for-GAD. Second-best (C): A reasonable conservative move, but it postpones a transition she is clinically ready for. (D) Monthly is too large a jump straight from weekly; tapering should be graded. (B) Holding weekly until full remission risks fostering dependence on the therapy structure and works against the autonomy the protocol is trying to build.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST captures the durable mechanism of change Tessa is internalizing?
options: Her catastrophic predictions have been disconfirmed enough times that she no longer believes them
Her relationship with uncertainty has shifted — she can notice the urge to control it and choose not to act on it
She has built relaxation and grounding skills that reliably down-regulate her physiological arousal
She has restructured her cognitive distortions into more balanced, evidence-based thoughts
questions.explanation: Best (B): For GAD specifically, the durable change is a new relationship with uncertainty — the *intolerance* is the engine, and loosening it generalizes across every domain she worries about. Second-best (A): True at the level of individual predictions, but new content always appears; without (B), each new worry restarts the cycle. (D) Restructuring is a vehicle for change, not the durable mechanism that survives novel stressors. (C) Skills help in the moment but, like (A), depend on (B) to keep working when life produces something genuinely uncertain.

sections.heading: The Golden Rule
content: Safety -> Rapport -> Least Assumptive -> Within Scope

sections.heading: 4-Step Decision Framework
content: 1. Check safety first: suicidal ideation, homicidal ideation, psychosis, abuse, severe impairment, or medical risk move to the front.
2. Early in the case, prioritize reflection, clarification, and assessment over advice or interpretation.
3. If the client asks what to do, explore meaning and context before jumping to direction.
4. When two answers seem right, choose the one that is more exploratory, less assumptive, and more client-centered.

sections.heading: Most Common Test Traps
content: Missing safety because the client sounds calm or vague.
Jumping to diagnosis before enough information is gathered.
Choosing an answer that acts outside counselor scope.
Picking the answer that sounds most active instead of most clinically appropriate.

sections.heading: Rapid Pattern Recognition
content: GAD = chronic, diffuse worry across domains.
Panic Disorder = sudden surges of fear plus catastrophic interpretation of body sensations.
MDD = depressed mood and/or loss of interest with functional impairment.
Bipolar spectrum = episodic mood shifts, especially decreased need for sleep and increased energy.
PTSD = trauma exposure plus intrusion, avoidance, and threat-related symptoms.
OCD = obsessions plus compulsions aimed at reducing distress or preventing feared outcomes.

sections.heading: When Two Answers Both Look Good
content: Pick the answer that builds alliance, gathers more information, and stays inside the counselor’s role.
Avoid answers that overpromise, overinterpret, or skip steps.

sections.heading: Final Reminder
content: You are not trying to sound smart. You are trying to think like a careful, ethical, entry-level clinician.
